items.text: Runs in the radial (spiral) groove on the back of the humerus
items.explain: It lies in the groove with the profunda brachii vessels.

items.text: Supplies extensor carpi radialis longus
items.explain: The radial nerve supplies the extensor muscles of the forearm.

items.text: Winds around the surgical neck of the humerus
items.explain: That is the axillary nerve. The radial nerve winds around the shaft, in the radial groove.

items.text: Is formed from the anterior rami of C7 and C8 only
items.explain: It is the continuation of the posterior cord and carries fibres from C5 to T1.

items.text: Injury in the radial groove causes wrist drop
items.explain: The wrist extensors are paralysed, so the wrist hangs flexed.

items.text: Passes behind the medial epicondyle of the humerus
items.explain: This is where it can be felt and hurt at the elbow.

items.text: Supplies the lateral two lumbricals
items.explain: The median nerve supplies the lateral two. The ulnar nerve supplies the medial two.

items.text: Supplies adductor pollicis
items.explain: Adductor pollicis is supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.

items.text: Passes deep to the flexor retinaculum through the carpal tunnel
items.explain: It passes superficial to the retinaculum, through Guyon's canal. The median nerve is in the carpal tunnel.

items.text: It is the most commonly fractured carpal bone
items.explain: A fall on the outstretched hand typically fractures it.

items.text: Its blood supply enters mainly at the proximal pole
items.explain: The blood supply enters distally and runs proximally.

items.text: A fracture through the waist can cause avascular necrosis of the proximal fragment
items.explain: The proximal fragment is cut off from its blood supply.

items.text: Tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox suggests a scaphoid fracture
items.explain: The scaphoid forms the floor of the snuffbox.

items.text: It articulates with the ulna
items.explain: It articulates with the radius, not the ulna, together with the lunate, capitate, trapezium and trapezoid.

items.text: It has three lobes
items.explain: Upper, middle and lower lobes.

items.text: It has a cardiac notch
items.explain: The cardiac notch is a feature of the left lung.

items.text: It has an oblique and a horizontal fissure
items.explain: The horizontal fissure separates the upper and middle lobes.

items.text: Its main bronchus is shorter, wider and more vertical than the left
items.explain: This is why inhaled foreign bodies lodge more often on the right.

items.text: It has a lingula
items.explain: The lingula belongs to the upper lobe of the left lung.

items.text: Granular cells secrete renin
items.explain: Granular (juxtaglomerular) cells store and release renin.

items.text: Macula densa cells secrete renin
items.explain: The macula densa senses the tubular fluid. Renin comes from the granular cells.

items.text: The macula densa senses sodium chloride delivery in the distal tubule
items.explain: This signal adjusts afferent arteriolar tone and renin release.

items.text: Granular cells are modified smooth muscle cells of the efferent arteriole
items.explain: They are mainly in the wall of the afferent arteriole.

items.text: The descending limb is highly permeable to water
items.explain: Water leaves along the osmotic gradient, so the fluid becomes concentrated.

items.text: The thick ascending limb is permeable to water
items.explain: It is impermeable to water, which dilutes the tubular fluid.

items.text: The thick ascending limb reabsorbs sodium through the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter
items.explain: This transporter drives the countercurrent multiplier.

items.text: Loop diuretics such as furosemide block this cotransporter
items.explain: That is why they are such powerful diuretics.

items.text: Fluid entering the distal tubule is hypertonic to plasma
items.explain: It is hypotonic, because salt is removed without water in the thick ascending limb.

questions.q: About glomerular filtration rate and clearance:

items.text: Inulin clearance can be used to measure GFR
items.explain: Inulin is freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted.

items.text: A normal GFR in a healthy adult is about 125 mL/min
items.explain: This is about 180 L a day.

items.text: Creatinine is freely filtered and not reabsorbed
items.explain: This is why creatinine clearance approximates GFR.

items.text: The clearance of glucose in a healthy person equals the GFR
items.explain: Glucose is fully reabsorbed at normal plasma levels, so its clearance is about zero.

items.text: The hypothalamus is the main integrating centre for temperature control
items.explain: It receives input from skin and core thermoreceptors.

items.text: Sweating is stimulated by sympathetic cholinergic fibres
items.explain: Sweat glands are the exception: the sympathetic fibres release acetylcholine.

items.text: Shivering is triggered when core temperature rises
items.explain: Shivering is triggered by cold and generates heat.

items.text: When air temperature is above skin temperature, evaporation is the main route of heat loss
items.explain: Radiation and conduction then add heat instead of removing it.

items.text: The fibres are multinucleated
items.explain: They form by fusion of many myoblasts.

items.text: The nuclei lie at the periphery, just under the sarcolemma
items.explain: Cardiac muscle has central nuclei.

items.text: Intercalated discs are a feature of skeletal muscle
items.explain: Intercalated discs are a feature of cardiac muscle.

items.text: The fibres show cross-striations
items.explain: The A and I bands give the striped appearance.

items.text: The fibres are branched
items.explain: Skeletal muscle fibres are long, unbranched cylinders. Cardiac muscle branches.
